title: Erdős Problem #784: Sieving Sets with Bounded Reciprocal Sums
description: Given C > 0, does there exist c > 0 such that sets A with Σ 1/n ≤ C leave ≫ x/(log x)^c unsieved elements? Answer: YES for C ≤ 1, NO for C > 1.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős Problem #784 studies the fundamental question of how effectively a set $A$ with bounded reciprocal sum $\sum_{n \in A} 1/n \leq C$ can sieve the integers. The problem traces to Andrzej Schinzel and George Szekeres (1959), who constructed sets showing the $x/(\log x)^c$ bound is the natural boundary. Imre Ruzsa (1982) made the decisive breakthrough: he proved the lower bound $H_1(x) \geq K \cdot x/\log x$ for the critical case $C = 1$, and showed the answer is NO for $C > 1$ by establishing $H_C(x) = x^{e^{1-C}+o(1)}$ — a sublinear growth rate when $C > 1$. Éric Saias (1998) closed the $C = 1$ case by proving the matching upper bound $H_1(x) \leq K \cdot x/\log x$, 16 years after Ruzsa's lower bound. Most recently, Andreas Weingartner (2025) gave precise asymptotics for all $C > 1$: $H_C(x) \asymp x^{e^{1-C}}/\log x$, specifying the $\log$ correction factor. The result reveals a sharp phase transition at $C = 1$: below this threshold, sieving is too constrained to eliminate many elements; above it, sieving becomes powerful enough to leave only a sublinear residue.
overview.problemStatement: Let C > 0. Does there exist c > 0 (depending on C) such that, for all sufficiently large x, if A ⊆ [1,x] has Σ_{n∈A} 1/n ≤ C then #{m ≤ x : a ∤ m for all a ∈ A} ≫ x/(log x)^c?
overview.text: Given C > 0, does there exist c > 0 such that sets A with Σ 1/n ≤ C leave ≫ x/(log x)^c unsieved elements? Answer: YES for C ≤ 1, NO for C > 1.
overview.proofStrategy: The answer depends critically on whether C ≤ 1 or C > 1. For C ≤ 1, the reciprocal sum constraint is strong enough that a polynomial-in-log bound holds. For C = 1 specifically, H₁(x) ≍ x/log x. For C > 1, the constraint is too weak: H_C(x) ≍ x^{e^{1-C}}/log x, which is sublinear and doesn't satisfy any polynomial-log bound.
keyInsights: The transition point is C = 1—a sharp phase transition in sieving behavior
For C < 1, the union bound gives a linear lower bound (1-C)x, so any c works
For C = 1, H₁(x) ≍ x/log x is the tight asymptotic (Ruzsa lower, Saias upper)
For C > 1, H_C(x) ≍ x^{α}/log x where α = e^{1-C} < 1—sublinear growth
The exponent α = e^{1-C} comes from analyzing optimal sieving sets
Schinzel-Szekeres showed x/(log x)^c bound is best possible for C = 1

sections.title: Basic Definitions
sections.summary: Defines reciprocal sum Σ 1/n for a set A, the sieved set of elements not divisible by any a ∈ A, and the sieving function H_C(x).
sections.mathContext: $\text{reciprocalSum}(A) = \sum_{n \in A} 1/n$; $\text{sievedSet}(A, x) = \{m \leq x : a \nmid m \text{ for all } a \in A\}$; $H_C(x) = \min\{|\text{sievedSet}(A,x)| : \sum_{A} 1/n \leq C\}$.

sections.title: The Question
sections.summary: Formalizes the main question: Does H_C(x) ≫ x/(log x)^c for some c depending on C?
sections.mathContext: $\text{HasPolynomialLogBound}(C) :\iff \exists c > 0, \exists K > 0, \forall x \geq 2: H_C(x) \geq K \cdot x/(\log x)^c$.

sections.title: The Case C = 1
sections.summary: States Ruzsa's lower bound and Saias's upper bound giving H₁(x) ≍ x/log x. Includes Weingartner's precise asymptotic constant c ≈ 0.878.
sections.mathContext: Ruzsa (1982): $H_1(x) \geq K_1 \cdot x/\log x$. Saias (1998): $H_1(x) \leq K_2 \cdot x/\log x$. Combined: $H_1(x) \asymp x/\log x$ with $c = 1$.

sections.title: The Case 0 < C < 1
sections.summary: The trivial case: union bound gives (1-C)x, which beats any polynomial-log bound. Answer is YES for all c.
sections.mathContext: For $C < 1$: at most $\sum_{a \in A} \lfloor x/a \rfloor \leq Cx$ elements are sieved, so $\geq (1-C)x$ survive — linear growth trivially dominates $x/(\log x)^c$.

sections.title: The Case C > 1
sections.summary: Ruzsa's negative answer: H_C(x) ≍ x^{e^{1-C}}/log x. Since e^{1-C} < 1 for C > 1, this is sublinear—no polynomial-log bound exists.
sections.mathContext: For $C > 1$: $\alpha = e^{1-C} < 1$, so $H_C(x) \asymp x^\alpha/\log x = o(x/(\log x)^c)$ for any $c > 0$. The sublinear exponent kills any polynomial-log bound.

sections.title: Schinzel-Szekeres Example
sections.summary: The 1959 construction showing the x/(log x)^c bound is best possible (up to the value of c).
sections.mathContext: Schinzel-Szekeres: $\forall c > 0, \exists A$ with $\sum 1/n \leq 1$ and $|\text{sievedSet}(A,x)| \leq 2x/(\log x)^c$. This shows the log-polynomial form is tight.

sections.title: The Trivial Cases
sections.summary: If 1 ∈ A, all elements are divisible. Hence we assume 1 ∉ A (validSet requires a ≥ 2).
sections.mathContext: Since $1 \mid m$ for all $m$, including 1 in $A$ trivially sieves everything. The `validSet` predicate requires $a \geq 2$ to avoid this degeneracy.

sections.title: Connection to Dense Divisors
sections.summary: Connection to Problem #542 and the phase transition principle for reciprocal sum control of sieving.
sections.mathContext: Dense divisor problems study the distribution of integers with many small divisors — the dual perspective to sieving. The phase transition at $C = 1$ mirrors phenomena in probabilistic number theory.

sections.title: Complete Answer
sections.summary: Combines all cases: YES for C ≤ 1, NO for C > 1. The transition at C = 1 is sharp.

sections.title: Main Problem Statement
sections.summary: Complete formalization with both asymptotic formulas and the dichotomous answer to the original question.
sections.mathContext: Packages all results: $H_1(x) \asymp x/\log x$, $H_C(x) \asymp x^{e^{1-C}}/\log x$ for $C > 1$, and the YES/NO dichotomy at $C = 1$. 5 axioms encode results spanning 1982-2025.

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #784 is SOLVED. The answer is YES for 0 < C ≤ 1 and NO for C > 1. For C = 1, H₁(x) ≍ x/log x (Ruzsa-Saias). For C > 1, H_C(x) ≍ x^{e^{1-C}}/log x (Ruzsa-Weingartner), which is sublinear.
conclusion.implications: This establishes a sharp phase transition at C = 1 in the sieving behavior of sets with bounded reciprocal sums. The result connects reciprocal sums (a measure of 'density' of divisors) to the number of unsieved elements, with deep implications for analytic number theory.
openQuestions: What is the exact asymptotic constant for H₁(x) ~ c · x/log x? (Weingartner conjectures c ≈ 0.878)
What are the lower-order terms in the asymptotic expansion?
How do these results extend to weighted sieving?
